title: The friendship paradox
text: Social scientists have noticed a curious pattern: on average, your friends have more friends than you {{1}}. This 'friendship paradox' is not an insult {{2}} at your social life but simple mathematics. Popular people appear in more people's lists of friends, so when you sample friends randomly, you {{3}} up oversampling popular people. The same logic {{4}} why your sexual partners' partners seem busier, why co-authors have more publications than you, and why the people you follow online seem to lead richer lives. Researchers {{5}} that the effect can distort our judgement: we compare ourselves with an unusually glittering sample of humanity and find ourselves {{6}}. The paradox even has practical {{7}}: during a flu outbreak, checking the friends of randomly chosen people detects epidemics weeks earlier, because well-connected individuals {{8}} infections first. Sometimes being average has its {{9}}.

title: The lost art of the weekend

The causes are familiar: smartphones that make us permanently {{3}}, workplaces that praise availability, and workloads that quietly expand. What is less familiar is the cost. Doctors link overwork to poor sleep, weakened immunity and {{4}} relationships; economists find that long hours beyond a certain point produce no extra output at all. Some countries have experimented with legal limits on out-of-hours contact, with {{5}} results: in France, employees have had a 'right to disconnect' since 2017. Companies, meanwhile, discover that rested employees are more, not less, {{6}}. Protecting the weekend, researchers insist, is not laziness but {{7}} for sustainable work — and it works best when it is {{8}} from the top.

title: Why we talk to ourselves
text: Talking to yourself used to be a sign to worry {{1}}, but psychologists now see it as a sign of intelligence. Studies show that self-talk works best in the second person: telling yourself 'You can do this' produces better results in difficult tasks {{4}} saying 'I can do this', perhaps because you hear it as advice from a coach. The tone matters as much as the words — {{5}} self-criticism tends to undermine performance. Researchers recommend instructional self-talk for complex {{6}} ('slowly, smooth movements') and motivational self-talk for endurance ('keep {{7}}'). Far from being a symptom, talking to yourself appears to be one of the mind's most {{8}} tools.

title: Cities that never sleep?
text: Night-time economies have become a measure of urban {{1}}, and cities compete to advertise how much happens after dark. Yet researchers studying night workers tell a more complicated story. title: The comeback of the cassette
text: Music formats rarely get second {{1}}, but the cassette tape is an exception. Industry observers are cautious about the numbers: cassettes remain a rounding error compared with streaming, and much of the revival is {{4}} to collectors rather than listeners. In an age of infinite playlists, constraints have become a luxury. The lesson, one label executive suggests, is that convenience does not {{6}} replace connection. Formats survive when they mean something, and meaning is the one thing the industry has never {{7}} to manufacture. Whether the cassette's comeback {{8}} depends, as ever, on the music.

title: Should we tax sugar?
text: When the United Kingdom introduced a tax on sugary drinks, critics predicted job losses and {{1}} protests about the nanny state. Three years later, the evidence suggests otherwise. Opponents still argue that such taxes are unfair, {{4}} poorer households hardest, since they spend a larger share of income on soft drinks. Supporters respond that the health benefits also flow disproportionately to those households, {{5}} diabetes is most common. Other countries have adopted the {{6}} with variations, from milkshake exemptions to fruit-juice bans. Debates continue about the {{7}} of evidence required before such a policy is justified. What is not disputed is that reformulation happened faster than decades of advice {{8}}.

title: The right to repair

title: What your accent says about you
text: Accent discrimination is one of the last openly tolerated prejudices, according to sociolinguists. The bias begins astonishingly early: children as young as five prefer to befriend speakers of high-status accents. Historically, broadcasters were required to adopt standard pronunciation, a rule that survived until the 1970s and whose {{2}} still shapes hiring in some industries. Researchers note that accent prejudice is really class prejudice by {{3}}, since accents map tightly onto social geography. Changing an accent is possible, but many refuse, {{4}} the cost as too high to their sense of identity. But the direction of travel is clear, and the days of the single 'proper' way to sound appear to be {{7}}. What remains is a simple test: if the words are right, the voice should not {{8}}.

title: The hidden price of free
text: The most profitable word in the digital economy is 'free'. We {{1}} nothing for search engines, maps and video calls, and we have quietly concluded that the internet runs on generosity. Your clicks, pauses and midnight searches are {{4}} into a profile that predicts what you will buy, watch and believe, and those predictions are auctioned to advertisers in {{5}} of a second. None of this is illegal, and much of it is {{6}} useful: free maps really did beat the paper versions, and free video calls changed family life. The trouble is subtler. Systems built to hold attention do not distinguish between the attention {{7}} on a documentary and the attention swallowed by outrage, so the feed quietly fills with whatever {{8}} hardest. 'Free', in other words, has a price; it is simply charged somewhere you cannot see.

title: In defence of boredom
text: Boredom has a bad {{1}}, and most of us will do almost anything to avoid it. Given the {{2}} of an empty afternoon, we reach for the phone before the feeling has even properly arrived. That reflex looks modern, but laboratory work has long shown how far people will go to escape their own thoughts: in one famous study, volunteers left alone for fifteen minutes chose to {{3}} themselves with mild electric shocks rather than sit quietly. The smartphone has made boredom {{6}} extinct, and few of us mourn. Yet at the first {{7}} of an idle moment we now scroll, and the mental space where ideas used to form is quietly leased out. title: How maps lie
text: Every map {{1}} three problems at once: projection, scale and selection. Flatten the round Earth onto a sheet of paper and something must {{2}} way. Gerardus Mercator's sixteenth-century compromise {{3}} navigators handsomely for four centuries, but at a price: on his grid, Greenland balloons {{4}} beyond its true size, while Africa, which could hold it fourteen times over, shrinks towards insignificance. It shows {{6}} passengers actually need — which line, which change, how many stops — and generations of tourists have been astonished by the real distances their journeys covered underground. text: The obituary of the high street has been written {{1}} times, and for understandable reasons. text: Almost everyone notices that time {{1}} up as we get older: childhood summers stretched without end, while a recent year can pass in what feels like weeks. title: In praise of libraries
text: The public library may be the most quietly {{1}} invention of civic life, and the easiest to take for granted. The librarian who {{5}} a bewildered teenager towards the right shelf performs a service no search engine replicates, and study after study {{6}} what regulars know: loan numbers may wobble, but {{7}} keeps rising, because the need for warm, free, unworried public space does not fade. A city, as the saying goes, ends up with the libraries it {{8}} — and the ones that survive their budget rounds tend to be busier than ever, full of toddlers, teenagers, job applicants and pensioners, all borrowed at the price of nothing at all.

text: A song {{1}} itself in the mind, replays for hours and refuses eviction: researchers call these sticky tunes {{2}}, and surveys {{3}} that roughly ninety per cent of us are regularly visited. Curiously, the phenomenon says something flattering about us: a mind that rehearses music involuntarily is a mind built for patterns — the same machinery, pointed elsewhere, that learns languages and does arithmetic in the shower.

text: Second-hand shopping has {{1}} its dusty image and become one of retail's growth stories.
